blocks.html: The ruse of this rogue is marvellous, and such that, if ever a malefactor could deserve some excuse for being excellent and sovereign in his kind of artifice and wickedness, this one would be worthy of it above all others: being another Phrynondas, of whom Aristophanes speaks, or a true Sisyphus,

notes.original: l. ad beſtias D. de pœn.
notes.gloss: Those condemned to the beasts are not to be released to please the crowd; but if they are of such strength or skill that they may worthily be exhibited to the Roman people, the governor is to consult the emperor — the malefactor's excellence in his kind earning him a reprieve, which is Coras's ironic point.

notes.citation: A Latin hexameter on Sisyphus — source not identified; it adapts Homer, Iliad 6.153, where Sisyphus is "the craftiest of men" (ὃ κέρδιστος γένετ' ἀνδρῶν)
notes.original: Syſiphus in terris, quo non aſtutior alter.
notes.gloss: The line is not in the Ilias Latina in this form; it may be a humanist rendering or Coras's own.

blocks.html: A Sisyphus on earth, than whom none other more cunning (Sisyphus in terris, quo non astutior alter).

Inasmuch as the substitution being already discovered, he nevertheless knew so well how to impose upon the Judges, nay, even upon the said de Rols, whose husband he always said he was, that the Judges in effect released him by an interlocutory order upon contrary facts; and the woman again received him as Martin Guerre her husband.
